paragraphs: A FIFTH need, which shows the usefulness of a senate, is a due sense of national character. Without a select and stable part of the government, the esteem of foreign powers will be forfeited by an uninformed and changeable policy arising from the causes already mentioned. In addition, the national councils will lack that sensitivity to the opinion of the world, which is perhaps as necessary to deserve the world's respect and confidence as it is to obtain them.

Attention to the judgment of other nations is important to every government for two reasons. The first is that, whatever the merits of a particular plan or measure, it is desirable on various grounds that it appear to other nations to be the product of a wise and honorable policy. The second is that in doubtful cases, particularly where the national councils may be bent by some strong passion or momentary interest, the presumed or known opinion of the impartial world may be the best guide to follow. What has America not lost for want of a character with foreign nations? And how many errors and follies would she have avoided, if the justice and propriety of her measures had in every instance first been tested by the light in which they would probably appear to the unbiased part of mankind?

Yet however necessary a sense of national character may be, it is plain that a numerous and changeable body can never have enough of it. It can be found only in a number so small that each individual receives a real share of the praise and blame for public measures, or in an assembly so durably invested with public trust that the pride and importance of its members are bound up with the reputation and prosperity of the community. The half-yearly representatives of Rhode Island would probably have been little affected, in their deliberations on the unjust measures of that State, by arguments drawn from how such measures would look to foreign nations, or even to the sister States. Yet it can hardly be doubted that if the agreement of a select and stable body had been required, regard for national character alone would have prevented the calamities under which that misguided people is now suffering.

I add, as a SIXTH defect, the lack in some important cases of proper responsibility of the government to the people. This comes from the very frequency of elections which in other cases produces such responsibility. This remark will perhaps seem not only new but paradoxical. Yet when explained, it must be acknowledged to be as undeniable as it is important.

To be reasonable, responsibility must be limited to matters within the power of the party held responsible. To be effective, it must relate to operations of that power on which the constituents can readily form a proper judgment. The objects of government may be divided into two general classes. One depends on measures that each have an immediate and noticeable effect. The other depends on a succession of well-chosen and well-connected measures, whose effect is gradual and perhaps unobserved. The importance of the second kind to the collective and lasting welfare of every country needs no explanation. And yet it is clear that an assembly elected for so short a term that it can provide only one or two links in a chain of measures on which the general welfare may essentially depend ought not to answer for the final result. A steward or tenant engaged for one year could not justly be made to answer for improvements that could not be completed in less than half a dozen years. Nor can the people estimate the SHARE of influence that their annual assemblies may each have had on events resulting from the mixed transactions of several years. It is difficult enough to keep the members of a NUMEROUS body personally responsible even for those acts of the body that have an immediate, separate and obvious effect on its constituents.

The proper remedy for this defect must be an additional body in the legislative department. Having enough permanence to provide for objects that require continued attention and a train of measures, it can be justly and effectively held answerable for achieving those objects.

So far I have considered the circumstances that show the need for a well-constructed Senate only as they relate to the representatives of the people. To a people as little blinded by prejudice or corrupted by flattery as those I address, I do not hesitate to add that such an institution may sometimes be necessary as a defense of the people against their own temporary errors and delusions. The calm and deliberate judgment of the community ought, in all governments, and actually will, in all free governments, prevail in the end over the views of its rulers. Even so, there are particular moments in public affairs when the people, stirred up by some irregular passion or some illicit advantage, or misled by the artful misrepresentations of interested men, may call for measures that they themselves will afterward be the first to lament and condemn. In these critical moments, how beneficial will be the interference of some temperate and respectable body of citizens, to check the misguided course and to hold back the blow the people are aiming at themselves, until reason, justice and truth can regain their authority over the public mind! What bitter anguish the people of Athens might often have escaped, if their government had contained so provident a safeguard against the tyranny of their own passions! Popular liberty might then have escaped the lasting reproach of decreeing hemlock to the same citizens one day and statues the next.

It may be suggested that a people spread over a wide region cannot, like the crowded inhabitants of a small district, be subject to the infection of violent passions or to the danger of uniting in pursuit of unjust measures. I am far from denying that this is a distinction of special importance. On the contrary, I tried in an earlier paper to show that it is one of the principal recommendations of a confederated republic. At the same time, this advantage should not be taken to make additional precautions unnecessary. It may even be remarked that the same wide situation that will spare the people of America some of the dangers of smaller republics will expose them to a different problem: they may stay for a longer time under the influence of those misrepresentations that the combined effort of interested men may succeed in spreading among them.

It adds considerable weight to all these considerations to recall that history shows no long-lived republic that did not have a senate. Sparta, Rome and Carthage are in fact the only states to which that description applies. In each of the first two there was a senate for life. The constitution of the senate in the last is less well known. Circumstantial evidence makes it probable that it did not differ in this respect from the other two. It is at least certain that it had some quality or other that made it an anchor against popular fluctuations, and that a smaller council drawn from the senate was appointed for life and filled its own vacancies. These examples are as unfit for imitation as they are repugnant to the character of America. Nevertheless, when compared with the short and turbulent existence of other ancient republics, they are very instructive proofs of the need for some institution that will blend stability with liberty. I am not unaware of the circumstances that distinguish the American government from other popular governments, ancient as well as modern, and that make extreme caution necessary in reasoning from one case to the other. But after giving this consideration its due weight, it can still be maintained that there are many points of likeness that make these examples worth our attention. Many of the defects that, as we have seen, can be supplied only by a senatorial institution are common to a numerous assembly frequently elected by the people and to the people themselves. There are others peculiar to the assembly, which require the control of such an institution. The people can never willfully betray their own interests, but they may possibly be betrayed by the representatives of the people. And the danger will plainly be greater where the whole legislative trust is lodged in the hands of one body of men than where the agreement of separate and dissimilar bodies is required for every public act.

The difference most relied on between the American republic and other republics lies in the principle of representation. It is the pivot on which the American government turns, and it is supposed to have been unknown to the others, or at least to the ancient ones. The use made of this difference in the reasoning of former papers will have shown that I am disposed neither to deny that it exists nor to undervalue its importance. I feel the less restraint, therefore, in observing that the position that the ancient governments were ignorant of representation is by no means exactly true in the broad sense commonly given to it. Without entering into a discussion that would be out of place here, I will point to a few known facts in support of what I say.

Even in the purest democracies of Greece, the people did not carry out many of the executive functions themselves. Those functions were performed by officers whom the people elected, who REPRESENTED the people in their EXECUTIVE capacity.

Before the reform of Solon, Athens was governed by nine Archons, ELECTED ANNUALLY BY THE PEOPLE AT LARGE. How much power was delegated to them seems to be left in great obscurity. After that period we find an assembly, first of four, and afterward of six hundred members, ELECTED ANNUALLY BY THE PEOPLE. It PARTIALLY represented them in their LEGISLATIVE capacity, since its members were not only associated with the people in the function of making laws but also had the exclusive right of originating legislative proposals to the people. The senate of Carthage, too, whatever its power or the length of its appointment, appears to have been ELECTIVE, by the votes of the people. Similar instances might be found in most, if not all, of the popular governments of antiquity.

Lastly, in Sparta we meet the Ephori, and in Rome the Tribunes: two bodies, small in numbers, but ELECTED ANNUALLY BY THE WHOLE BODY OF THE PEOPLE and regarded as the REPRESENTATIVES of the people, almost in a PLENIPOTENTIARY capacity. The Cosmi of Crete were also ELECTED ANNUALLY BY THE PEOPLE. Some authors have considered them an institution analogous to those of Sparta and Rome, with this difference only: in electing that representative body, the right to vote was given to only a part of the people.

In answer to all these arguments, suggested by reason, illustrated by examples and backed by our own experience, the suspicious opponent of the Constitution will probably be content to repeat that a senate not appointed directly by the people, and serving a term of six years, must gradually gain a dangerous preeminence in the government and finally transform it into a tyrannical aristocracy.

The general answer to this should be enough: liberty may be endangered by the abuses of liberty as well as by the abuses of power; there are numerous instances of the former as well as of the latter; and it is the former, rather than the latter, that the United States apparently has most to fear. But a more particular reply can be given.

Before such a revolution could be brought about, the Senate, it should be observed, would have to corrupt itself first. It would next have to corrupt the State legislatures, then the House of Representatives, and finally the people at large. It is evident that the Senate must be corrupted first before it can attempt to establish tyranny. It cannot carry on the attempt without corrupting the State legislatures, because the periodic change of members would otherwise renew the whole body. Unless it used the means of corruption with equal success on the House of Representatives, the opposition of that coequal branch of the government would inevitably defeat the attempt. And unless it corrupted the people themselves, a succession of new representatives would soon restore everything to its original order. Can anyone seriously persuade himself that the proposed Senate could, by any means within the reach of human skill, arrive at the goal of a lawless ambition through all these obstacles?

If reason condemns the suspicion, experience pronounces the same verdict. The constitution of Maryland furnishes the most fitting example. The Senate of that State is elected, as the federal Senate will be, indirectly by the people, and for a term only one year shorter than that of the federal Senate. It is also distinguished by the remarkable prerogative of filling its own vacancies within the term of its appointment, and it is not subject to any rotation like the one provided for the federal Senate. There are some other lesser differences that would expose the Maryland Senate to plausible objections that do not apply to the federal one. If the federal Senate really contained the danger that has been so loudly proclaimed, then some symptoms at least of a like danger ought by this time to have shown themselves in the Senate of Maryland. No such symptoms have appeared. On the contrary, the suspicions first held by men of the same description as those who view the corresponding part of the federal Constitution with terror have been gradually put to rest by the progress of the experiment. And the Maryland constitution is daily gaining, from the beneficial working of this part of it, a reputation that probably no other State in the Union will rival.

If anything could silence these suspicions, it ought to be the British example. The Senate there is not elected for six years and is not open to people of any family or fortune; it is a hereditary assembly of wealthy nobles. The House of Representatives there is not elected for two years by the whole body of the people; it is elected for seven years, and in very great proportion by a very small proportion of the people. Here, beyond question, we ought to see in full display the aristocratic usurpations and tyranny that are supposed to be played out in the United States at some future time. Unfortunately for the anti-federal argument, however, British history tells us that this hereditary assembly has been unable to defend itself against the continual encroachments of the House of Representatives, and that as soon as it lost the support of the monarch, it was actually crushed by the weight of the popular branch.

To the extent that antiquity can teach us anything on this subject, its examples support our reasoning. In Sparta the Ephori, the annual representatives of the people, proved more than a match for the senate for life; they gained on its authority continually and finally drew all power into their own hands. The Tribunes of Rome, who were the representatives of the people, prevailed, as is well known, in almost every contest with the senate for life, and in the end gained the most complete triumph over it. The fact is the more remarkable because the Tribunes had to be unanimous in every act, even after their number was increased to ten. It proves the irresistible force of that branch of a free government which has the people on its side. To these examples might be added that of Carthage. According to the testimony of Polybius, its senate, far from drawing all power into its vortex, had by the beginning of the second Punic War lost almost the whole of its original share.

These facts together are conclusive evidence that the federal Senate will never be able to turn itself, by gradual usurpations, into an independent and aristocratic body. But we are warranted in believing something more. Suppose such a revolution should ever happen, from causes that human foresight cannot guard against. Then the House of Representatives, with the people on their side, will always be able to restore the Constitution to its original form and principles. Against the force of the people's immediate representatives, nothing will be able to maintain even the constitutional authority of the Senate, except a display of enlightened policy and devotion to the public good that wins for it, alongside that branch of the legislature, the affection and support of the entire body of the people themselves.
